title: API Styles: REST, RPC, GraphQL
subtitle: Load one mobile order screen three different ways and see what each API style costs in round trips and bytes.
learn: How REST models resources and why it leans on HTTP verbs and caching
Why gRPC and protobuf suit fast service-to-service calls
How GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs, and what that costs the server
Why cursor pagination beats offset pagination on large, changing data
How to evolve an API without breaking existing clients
A simple rule for choosing a style for a given caller

steps.title: One screen, many needs
steps.body: A phone app needs to draw one order screen. It shows the order, the customer's name, and each item with its stock status. That data lives in two backend services: Orders and Inventory. How should the app ask for it? The best answer depends on who is calling and how far away they are. We assume the phone has a 60 ms round trip (RTT: the time for a request to go out and the answer to come back).
steps.idea: An API style is the agreed way a caller asks for data. The best style depends on who is calling.
steps.caption: The phone needs data held by two backend services.

steps.title: REST: resources and verbs
steps.body: REST treats each thing as a resource with its own URL. Verbs say what to do: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, DELETE removes. Status codes report the result (200 OK, 404 not found, 409 conflict). In the animation the phone sends one GET /orders/812 and gets the order back: one round trip. Assume an 18 KB JSON reply and 10 ms of server time per call, so 60 + 10 = 70 ms. GET is safe to repeat, so browsers and CDNs can cache it. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent (repeating them changes nothing more). POST is not, so payment APIs add an idempotency key.
steps.idea: REST maps things to URLs and actions to HTTP verbs. That makes it easy to cache and easy to test with curl.
steps.caption: One GET fetches one order: 1 trip, 70 ms.

steps.title: REST's chattiness problem
steps.body: The order reply holds only ids for the customer and items. So the phone needs more calls: the order, then the customer, then the stock. Each waits for the last, costing 60 ms of network plus 10 ms of server time. That is 3 x 70 = 210 ms. Running the last two in parallel still takes 2 round trips. Replies also carry fields the screen never shows (over-fetching), so the total reaches about 40 KB (assumed). Needing extra calls is under-fetching. Here the Orders service also serves customer data.
steps.idea: A fixed-shape resource forces extra calls (under-fetching) or unused bytes (over-fetching) when a screen needs a custom view.
steps.caption: Three calls, one after another, to build one screen.

steps.title: gRPC: fast calls between services
steps.body: Inside the data center, the gateway talks to Inventory with gRPC, a remote procedure call (RPC) framework. RPC means calling a function on another machine as if it were local. A .proto file defines the methods and typed messages. Protobuf packs them into compact binary, often 3-10x smaller than the same JSON (a rule of thumb). Many calls share one HTTP/2 connection. The animation shows one fast hop: 12 ms and a 5 KB reply. Two catches: browsers cannot call gRPC without a proxy, and the shared long-lived connection needs L7 or client-side load balancing.
steps.idea: gRPC gives up readable text and direct browser access. In return it is fast and strictly typed, which suits internal calls.
steps.caption: The gateway asks Inventory for stock over binary gRPC.

steps.title: GraphQL: ask for exactly what you need
steps.body: With GraphQL the phone sends one query to a single endpoint. The query names the exact fields it wants: order id, customer name, and each item's name and in-stock flag. The GraphQL server collects them from Orders and Inventory (a fan-out: one request splits into several), then returns only what was asked for. One round trip carries about 6 KB. Assume the fan-out takes 30 ms, so the screen loads in 60 + 30 = 90 ms instead of 210 ms.
steps.idea: GraphQL lets the client choose the response shape, so many calls collapse into one precise reply.
steps.caption: One query in; the server fans out to Orders and Inventory.

steps.title: The hidden costs of GraphQL
steps.body: That freedom moves work onto the server. Say a client asks for 100 orders, each with 10 items, each with stock. A naive server makes 1 call for the orders, 100 for their items and 1,000 for stock: over 1,100 backend calls from one query. This is the N+1 problem (one call for the list, then one more per item). Fix it by batching lookups. Queries are usually POSTs to one URL, so normal HTTP caching mostly does not apply. Teams cache by object id, or use persisted queries over GET. Add depth and cost limits so one query cannot overload the system.
steps.idea: GraphQL needs batching, query-cost limits and its own caching. The server pays for the client's freedom.
steps.caption: One deep query turns into over a thousand backend calls.

steps.title: Listing without loading everything
steps.body: Any list endpoint needs pagination, or it would return every row at once. Offset style (?limit=50&offset=100000) is simple, but the database must skip 100,000 rows each time. If rows are inserted meanwhile, pages shift and items repeat or vanish. Cursor style (?limit=50&after=ord_7f3a) resumes after the last row you saw. The cursor is an opaque token holding that row's sort key (for example created_at plus id), so the database jumps straight there using an index. Cost stays flat and pages stay stable. The trade-off: you can go next or previous, but not jump to page 40.
steps.idea: Use cursor pagination for large or changing lists. Keep offset for small, stable data.
steps.caption: Orders returns 50 rows plus a cursor for the next page.

steps.title: Changing an API without breaking callers
steps.body: Old app versions stay installed for years, so you cannot just change a response. Safe changes are additive: new optional fields or new endpoints. Breaking changes (rename, remove, change a type) need a new version, such as /v2/orders or a version header. Keep the old one until few people use it. The animation shows the old phone app on v1 and the web app on v2, both served at once. Protobuf lets you add fields but never reuse a field number. GraphQL marks fields deprecated, then removes them later.
steps.idea: Change APIs by adding, not breaking. When a break is unavoidable, run old and new versions side by side.
steps.caption: Old and new clients call different versions at the same time.

steps.title: Choosing a style
steps.body: Use REST for public, cacheable APIs that many unknown clients call. Use gRPC between your own services, where speed and strict contracts matter. Use GraphQL when several client types (phone, web) need different views of connected data. Many systems mix all three behind a gateway. Page lists with cursors and change APIs additively. A purpose-built endpoint (a backend-for-frontend) can also give a one-trip result without GraphQL.
steps.idea: Pick by caller: REST for the public, gRPC for internal hops, GraphQL for flexible client views.
steps.caption: Each style fits a different caller.

quiz.q: A phone on a 100 ms RTT network needs data that takes three dependent REST calls. What is the most direct fix for load time?
options: Compress the JSON with gzip
Switch the calls from GET to POST
Return the combined data in one call, for example via a GraphQL query or a purpose-built endpoint
Add more database replicas
quiz.why: Dependent calls cost one RTT each, about 300 ms here. Cutting the number of round trips helps far more than shrinking bytes.

quiz.q: Why does gRPC suit calls between your own backend services better than a public browser-facing API?
options: gRPC uses compact binary messages, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and typed generated clients, while browsers lack direct support
gRPC works natively in every browser
gRPC responses are cached by CDNs automatically
gRPC removes the need for a schema
quiz.why: Binary protobuf and HTTP/2 reduce size and latency, and the .proto contract gives strict types. Browsers need a proxy, so public APIs usually stay REST or GraphQL.

quiz.q: A GraphQL endpoint slows down after clients start requesting orders with nested items and reviews. Which is the likely cause and remedy?
options: HTTP verbs are wrong; switch to PUT
The schema is too small; add more types
Protobuf encoding is too large
N+1 resolver calls; batch lookups and add query depth or cost limits
quiz.why: Nested fields can trigger one backend call per parent item. Batching (such as a data loader) and cost limits keep fan-out under control.

quiz.q: A feed is paged with ?limit=20&offset=. While a user reads page 2, ten new posts are inserted at the top. What happens when they load page 3?
options: Nothing; offsets are stable
Some posts from page 2 appear again, because everything shifted down
Ten posts are skipped
The server returns an error
quiz.why: Inserts at the front shift every later row, so offset-based pages repeat items. A cursor anchored to the last seen id avoids this.

quiz.q: You must rename the field total to totalCents in a REST response used by apps you cannot force to update. What is the safest approach?
options: Rename it in place and announce the change
Delete total and return an error to old clients
Add totalCents alongside total, keep both, and remove total only after old clients are gone or in a new version
Change the field's type but keep its name
quiz.why: Additive changes do not break existing callers. Removal or rename is a breaking change that needs a transition period or a new version.

cheatsheet.def: Resources at URLs, acted on with HTTP verbs and status codes. Easy to cache and debug; fixed response shapes can cause over- or under-fetching.
RPC over HTTP/2 with a .proto contract and compact binary messages. Fast and strictly typed; best for internal service calls.
One endpoint where the client sends a query naming exact fields. Fewer round trips; needs batching, cost limits, and id-based caching.
Over-fetching returns unused fields; under-fetching forces extra calls because one response lacks needed data.
One query for a list plus one extra call per item. Fix by batching lookups or joining.
Resume from the last seen key (?after=id). Stable under inserts and constant cost, unlike large offsets.
Adding optional fields or endpoints. Does not break old clients; renames, removals, and type changes do.
Repeating the call has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT, and DELETE should be; POST usually is not, so use idempotency keys for payments.
